one_liner: Google's byte-oriented LZ77 codec: about 5x faster compression and 3x faster decompression than zlib -1, with larger output.
what_it_does: A C++ library (with a C wrapper in snappy-c.h) for whole-buffer compression in Snappy's own fixed bitstream format, not deflate, so it is not a drop-in for zlib. The main calls are snappy::Compress/Uncompress on std::string, RawCompress/RawUncompress on caller-sized arrays (MaxCompressedLength), Source/Sink and iovec variants, GetUncompressedLength in O(1), and IsValidCompressedBuffer for cheap validation. Streaming to files uses a separate framing format (framing_format.txt) with data checksums, which is optional and not part of the core specification.
how_it_is_fast: Input is cut into 64 KiB blocks; each is matched with a single 4-byte hash table of 16-bit offsets (up to 2^15 entries, CRC32 instruction as hash where available) and emitted as byte-aligned literal and copy tags with no entropy coding. A 'heuristic match skipping' rule widens the stride after every 32 bytes without a match, so incompressible data such as JPEG passes through quickly. The decoder translates tags through a lookup table and copies with unaligned 64/128-bit loads, plus SSSE3/NEON shuffle masks to expand short repeating patterns; BMI2 and x86/ARM CRC32 paths are picked at build time.
when_to_use: RPC payloads, cache values, column blocks and log records where CPU per byte matters more than ratio, or where peers already speak the Snappy format (it has compressed petabytes in Google production, per the README).
Mixed or partly incompressible data: the skip heuristic keeps throughput high on already-compressed content.
Untrusted input: the README says the decompressor is designed not to crash on corrupted or malicious input, and IsValidCompressedBuffer checks a buffer at least about 4x faster than decoding it.
Code that needs a zero-allocation compressor: v1.3.1 adds CompressionContext with a caller-provided workspace.
when_not_to_use: New designs free to choose a format: in the same lzbench 2.4 run, lz4 1.10.0 compresses faster (550 vs 457 MB/s) and decompresses about 3.9x faster (3832 vs 976 MB/s) at the same ratio, and zstd -1 gives much smaller output (34.53% vs 47.85%) at similar speed.
When ratio matters: output is 20-100% larger than zlib's fastest mode per the README (47.85% vs 36.45% of input on silesia.tar).
Inputs of 4 GiB or more in one call: Compress returns zero and writes nothing for inputs of 2^32 bytes or more; split the data or use the framing format.
32-bit targets on 1.3.x: issue #266 reports Snappy.LiteralLengthU32Overflow failing on i386 and armhf (corrupt input accepted as valid), a regression from 1.2.2 with no fix yet.
Big-endian or strict-alignment CPUs: the README warns it assumes little-endian and cheap unaligned loads and may run slower elsewhere.

integration.form: static lib (default) or shared lib via CMake (BUILD_SHARED_LIBS); C++ with a C API
integration.dependencies: none at runtime; bundled GoogleTest and Google Benchmark only for tests and benchmarks
integration.min_toolchain: C++11, CMake 3.10+; Clang is the supported compiler, GCC and MSVC best-effort
integration.platforms: x86, x86-64, ARMv7, AArch64 tuned (SSSE3, BMI2, CRC32, NEON paths); RISC-V improved in 1.3.1; other platforms portable but slower
integration.thread_safety: Free functions with no shared state are documented only implicitly; the header says a CompressionContext may be reused for sequential calls but must not be used from multiple threads at once.

gotchas: The CMake build compiles with -fno-rtti and -fno-exceptions, so code that subclasses snappy::Source/Sink against a shared libsnappy can fail to link with 'undefined symbol: typeinfo for snappy::Source' (open issue #184).
Compression level 2 (added in 1.2.1) is marked EXPERIMENTAL in snappy.h and may fall back to level 1 later; levels 3 and up are not supported.
MSVC builds older than /arch:AVX2 must set SNAPPY_HAVE_SSSE3, SNAPPY_HAVE_BMI2 and related macros by hand, or the fast paths stay off.
Versions before 1.2.2 could corrupt data when compressed size exceeded 4 GB (for example near-4 GB incompressible input), per NEWS.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Snappy when the Snappy format is required for interoperability or you are already on Google's stack; for a new choice, LZ4 matches its ratio with much faster decompression, zstd -1 gives a far better ratio at similar speed, and LZAV claims to beat it on both speed and ratio (first-party numbers).
verified_claims_summary: Independent lzbench 2.4 (gcc 15.2.0 release binary, single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, turbo off, silesia.tar): snappy 1.3.1 compresses at 457 MB/s and decompresses at 976 MB/s at 47.85% size versus zlib 1.3.2 -1 at 89.0 and 297 MB/s at 36.45%, about 5.1x and 3.3x faster with larger output (derived from page data). The README's 'order of magnitude faster than zlib's fastest mode' is a first-party claim on an unnamed Core i7.
status_note: Actively maintained by Google (v1.3.1, 2026-09-18) under BSD-3-Clause with a stable bitstream; Google says it will not accept build-system or platform changes outside its own configurations.
